Everyone Says Your Business Idea Is Great? Test This First

Customer discovery is checking, before you build, that real people have the problem you think they have. A friend's yes costs them nothing, so it can't tell you whether strangers will pay.

Watch on YouTube

About this video

This video shows how to validate a business idea with AI: why the usual questions fail (The Mom Test), what building first cost the IMVU team, jobs to be done (the milkshake case), and an evidence ladder from cheapest to dearest. It ends with a live run of the free Riskiest Guess Finder on an example idea, using ten real reviews of a planner already on sale.

Full transcript

0:00You have this great business idea, and your friends all say it's great. That's kind, but a friend's yes costs them nothing, so it can't tell you if strangers will pay. So then comes the question, what does tell you? Before you spend months building it? Most people assume you have to go and talk to strangers. And while there is truth to that, if you are like me, that sounds awkward and slow. You can start without that. In most cases, buyers of similar products have already left evidence, and the best part is, AI can read it for you. Later in this video I will take you through this free AI tool,

0:31the Riskiest Guess Finder, it finds and ranks the guesses an idea rests on and writes the cheapest test for it. Here it is on an example idea, a series of KDP planners, and you can also run it on yours. Just to show you, here's what building first can cost. Eric Ries co-founded a company called IMVU, and in a 2010 talk he said his team spent about six months building an add-on for instant-messaging apps. Then in his 2009 interview he described a tester who wouldn't even invite a friend to use the feature. The idea didn't hold up, and in his words

1:02they wound up having to throw all of that code away. Would anyone even have clicked a download button? His own answer was basically no. That six months wasted, taught what a cheaper test could have shown from the start. Your idea runs the same risk, and the belief behind it is usually that if people like it, it's wanted. But liking costs them nothing. Your idea is a prototype: test it on real customers before you build it. What guess does your idea rest on, how can AI get you evidence before you build, and which test should you run this week.

1:33But first, why the usual questions fail. Pitching your idea makes the conversation about you. And asking "would you buy this?", is asking about a future that costs someone nothing to promise. Both of those invite a kind person to be kind. it's the approach that goes wrong, not the people. So the easy guesses get tested, and the one that would kill the idea waits until it's built. Rob Fitzpatrick, wrote The Mom Test. It says you should ask about the past instead. Which is the same as looking at what buyers already did. Take the example idea.

2:04Weekly planner paperbacks, printed by Amazon only when someone orders one. The plan is a whole series, each book made for one kind of person. It's a typical example, you can find multiple youtube videos explaining how to do it. Underneath that sits a stack of guesses, like "freelancers search Amazon for planners", and "they would pick a design specifically made for them over a generic one". Each one feels true. Maybe one person even said they wanted exactly that, but one anecdote is not proof. Those guesses are called assumptions: what you believe about who has the problem, how badly, and what they do about it today.

2:36Checking your assumptions before you build it is customer discovery: finding out whether real people have the problem and what they would pay for it. Like the business model in my last video, testing an idea should be seen as a system. Time and access to customers run out, so you can't test everything. The signal worth trusting, is what people do. So your leverage point is the riskiest guess that's cheap to test. If it's wrong, everything resting on it cascades down with it: the product, the price, the pitch. Two laws help you find that guess.

3:06Law one: test where change is cheapest. A flaw found before you build costs a small test. But found after, it costs the whole build. Law two: measure behaviour, not opinion. Clayton Christensen told a story about a fast-food chain and how people "hired" its milkshakes, which is his jargon for "bringing a product into your life to get a job done". More shakes than you'd expect sold early in the day, to commuters, who hired one to fill a boring drive and keep hunger away. Parents, in the afternoon, hired it for a different job.

3:36Christensen calls this jobs to be done: people hire a product to make progress in a situation. The clue was behaviour: when it sold, and who was buying. Find the job, and the product, price and pitch follow. So where do you find that behaviour? Evidence comes like rungs on a ladder, cheapest first, and the cheapest rung needs nobody to talk to. Rung one is existing behaviour: what buyers of similar products already did and wrote. That used to mean going through everything customers said, by hand. Now, a language model can read a pile of reviews and group them into the

4:09struggles that keep coming back, in the customers' exact words. Here's a real run on real reviews of a planner already on sale. I pasted ten unhappy reviews into a free Claude chat and asked for the situations people were in. The more you give it, the more it can analyse. Claude came back with six situations. The three biggest each had three reviews: planning the weekend, expecting more room than it has, and a part failing from normal day to day use. Claude also flagged its own doubts. One review never mentions the weekend, so it was placed by inference, and some reviews contradict each other,

4:41like thick paper against thin. That's why you spot-check three against the originals: the sorting and counting are the model's work, so they can be wrong. An unhappy review is a customer describing the situation they were in. I've noticed this myself, reading reviews before buying, that when a product misses a big expectation, people usually explain why they're frustrated, not just that it was bad. Research on vacation-rental reviews found the same pattern: negative reviews tend to run long and describe disappointment when expectations weren't met. What people write after a product lets them down is closer to what they did than to just what they'd say.

5:12That's rung one of our ladder. Rung two goes further, because it creates behaviour that doesn't exist yet. That's a smoke test. It's a simple page offering a free sample of the product, with an email sign-up. Then a small ad or a community post sends people there. Now you can see what people do. AI builds the page and writes the ad. You put them live, set the spend and read the count, because that count is your evidence. Before you start, you set a pass line and a fail line. They're the counts that mean keep going, and the counts that mean stop and rethink. You set them first, so you can't talk yourself into a pass afterwards.

5:45One caution to keep in mind with the free tool. Here's my view, not research. An AI summary of reviews is not an actual customer, and neither is an AI playing one. Use AI to read real words and to prepare, but the real evidence still comes from what real people do. It gives you insight to what people said, not what they will do. Back to the example idea. Here's the free guess finder tool. Two sentences go in: weekly planner paperbacks for freelancers who work from home, plus the logic (or rather beliefs) behind the idea.

6:15What comes back is the test card. It holds five guesses with a risk score and a cost score for each, the ranked order, one test with a pass line and a fail line, and how to read the result. The first guess is that home-working freelancers have a week-organising problem bad enough that they'd buy a paper planner for it. The other four cover search, the specific design, repeat buying and how crowded the space is. The first guess, demand, comes back high risk and cheap to test. The ranking after demand is crowding, then the design claim, then search, then repeat buying.

6:47You might expect the design claim to come first, since it's the whole pitch, but it ranks third, because it costs more to test than demand or crowding. Demand beats crowding because crowding only matters if demand exists. So the leverage point is demand. Do freelancers who work from home really want a paper planner to fix their week? If that's wrong, the search, design and repeat-buying guesses fall with it. The test starts on rung one of the ladder, because this guess is about what buyers already do and complain about. It's about two to three hours of copying the reviews,

7:18or you can let AI collect them for you. Then it reads everything in one pass. Here's how you read the result. A pass means keep the guess and move on. A fail means change the idea, the customer or the claim. Anything in between means narrow the test, make it cheaper or step up on the ladder. The tool also gives an honest line, and I agree with it. No fully automated validation exists. A human has to act, but you don't have to talk to anyone to start. So the answer to the question from the start is behaviour. It starts with what buyers already did,

7:48and then moves to what they do when you offer something. Your move this week: run the Riskiest Guess Finder on your own idea. Fill in your pass and fail numbers before you look at anything. Your idea is an unverified prototype, no matter how great you and the people closest to you think it is. Test it on real customers before you build it. Look at the behaviour of your competitors' customers. The time spent verifying before building is cheap compared to the time put in to make and then remake it (or having to throw it all away after finding
